1: Welcome the group. Reverse headhunts (RHH) are a core part of business development, especially on contract and consulting desks, where we need conversations with senior technology leaders who are normally hard to reach. Today covers what an RHH is, why it works, who to target, how to run the call, and the outreach and weekly rhythm that keep your diary full. Ask everyone to have LinkedIn and their CRM open. Timing: 75 minutes including a role-play.
2: Set expectations: by the end of the session everyone should have a call structure, two question banks and an outreach message they can send this afternoon. Check the pre-work: who has their list of 10 decision makers? If anyone doesn’t, they’ll build it during the exercise.
3: A reverse headhunt flips the usual BD call. Instead of pitching services to a leader who gets ten vendor calls a day, you approach them as a senior candidate. People will always make time to talk about themselves. Stress that this is especially powerful on contract and consulting desks, where the real opportunity is often a project or team rather than one hire. Five minutes.
4: Ask the room which of these matters most for their desk. On contract and consulting, number 3 and number 6 tend to be the big ones: you learn where projects are stalling and position Stott and May as a delivery partner. Even if the leader isn’t hiring now, being seen as someone who wants to help them makes them far more likely to call you when they are. Five minutes.
5: Have people pull up their pre-work list of 10 decision makers and check it against these titles. Include leaders one level below the obvious buyer: today’s Director is next year’s VP, and they remember who called them first.
6: Steps 2 and 3 treat the leader as a candidate; step 4 is where they become a potential client. The move from 3 to 4 should feel natural: “You mentioned you’re leading the cloud migration. How’s delivery going?” Never skip step 5. A great conversation with no next step booked is a missed opportunity. Ask for referrals every time: senior leaders know other senior leaders. Ten minutes; model a call for the group if you can.
7: The original playbook asked for current salary. We’ve changed that to target package: asking a candidate’s current or past pay is illegal in New York City and many other US jurisdictions, and it applies to senior leaders too. The more you learn here, the more ways you have to position Stott and May as a partner. Don’t interrogate; pick the questions that fit the conversation and note the rest for next time.
8: These questions turn a career chat into a business conversation. The right-hand column is where opportunities come from. Log everything in the CRM so whoever speaks to that business next starts informed.
9: This is a tightened version of the team’s original template, about half the length. Fill the brackets with your market and real, recent placements from your desk or the wider business; ask your manager if you’re not sure what you can reference. Never claim placements or retained searches we don’t have; a senior leader will check. Personalise the first line wherever you can: a recent post, a promotion, a project they announced.
10: These are the activity standards from the original playbook. A reverse headhunt only pays off over time, so the tracking matters as much as the outreach. Everyone should leave with a tracker (CRM or spreadsheet) listing each leader, the date of the call, what you learned and the next follow-up date.
11: The “leader” should be friendly but busy, giving short answers until the caller earns more. The one measure of success is whether a follow-up meeting is booked by the end of the call. Afterwards, everyone sends the outreach message to at least five real leaders before the end of the day. Managers then run the same paired role-play on desk within the week.
12: Ask everyone to write at least three takeaways and pick the action they’ll do first. The last action matters: you can’t position Stott and May as a partner if you can’t explain every hiring model and practice we offer. Managers: check RHH numbers in the weekly activity review.
13: Open the floor for questions. Point to Module 07: once the client is engaged, client control is how you keep the process on your timeline.
